Secrets, database migrations, JAR files and third-party modules

01

The four things this lab adds to the pipeline: secrets, schema, modules and JARs

Gap 1

Secrets

The gateway's DB password, the API keys your deploy scans with, the runner's PAT. They configure the system but can't be committed. Where do they live: locally, in Compose, in the gateway, in CI?

Gap 2

The database

Your screens read and write tables. The schema lives in a Docker volume: nothing versions it, nothing deploys it. Today it becomes files in the repo, shipped by the same pipeline.

Gap 3

Third-party modules

MQTT drivers, charting modules, historians: .modl binaries the gateway needs at boot. Who versions them, how do they reach the gateway, who accepts the license?

Gap 4

JAR files

JDBC drivers and Java libraries your scripts call. In 8.3 some are config resources, some sit on the gateway classpath: both ship with the deploy.

Builds on the Lab 04 and 05 stackLocal, test and production gateways, the .env.example convention and the db-init/ folder. Routing is unchanged: push to main deploys test, a lab06-v* tag deploys production. lab06-release.yml is a thin caller of the one lab06-deploy.yml, so the steps you add today ship to both gateways.

Part 1: which values may never be committed, and where they live instead

02

Sort every value: public, per-environment or secret

Kind 1

Public

Port numbers, module lists, project names, timeouts, modules.json.

Committed, plain, in the repo
Kind 2

Per-environment

Gateway URLs, database names, container names. Same shape, different value per environment.

Committed defaults plus env vars or GitHub environment variables
Kind 3

Secret

Passwords, API keys, PATs, private keys, keystores. Anyone holding the value is you.

Never committed: .env, Docker secrets, secret providers, GitHub secrets
03

Why a pushed secret must be rotated, not just deleted

# Monday, 09:14: "just to make it work"
git commit -m "wire up historian"
+ IGNITION_API_KEY = "ak_live_9f3ce81b..."
# Monday, 09:40: "phew, removed it"
git commit -m "oops, remove key"
- IGNITION_API_KEY = "ak_live_9f3ce81b..."
# anyone, any clone, any time later:
git log -p | grep ak_live
+ IGNITION_API_KEY = "ak_live_9f3ce81b..."  # still there
The only correct response1. Rotate the credential, immediately. The old value is public now: make it worthless.
2. Then, optionally, scrub history (git filter-repo, BFG). On a shared remote that is best-effort: forks, clones and CI caches keep copies.
Deleting the line and force-pushing without rotating is theatre.
Prevention beats responseScanners catch the 09:14 commit before it lands: scripts/validate.sh scans the payload for known secret values locally, and gitleaks checks every commit of a PR in CI (wiring that job is a stretch goal).

Step through the leak everyone commits once, and why "removing" it fixes nothing. Monday 09:14: an API key is committed "just to make it work", and pushed. Monday 09:40: delete the line, commit, push. Crisis averted? No. Commits are immutable snapshots: the key sits in history, in every clone and fork. git log -p reads it right back. So: rotate first, scrub second, and add a scanner so the 09:14 commit never leaves a laptop again.

04

The secrets ladder: four rungs, from hardcoded to referenced

0
Hardcoded in the repoplaintext in docker-compose.yaml or committed config
Leaks into: Git history, every clone, every fork. Never acceptable.
1
Env vars via .env and Compose interpolationwhat labs 02 to 05 already do
Out of Git. Still leaks into: docker inspect, compose config, the process env.
2
File-based secretsfiles mounted read-only at /run/secrets/<name>
Not in inspect, not in the process env. A plaintext file on the host: the infra side owns and fills it.
3
Ignition 8.3 secret providersgateway config references a secret instead of containing it
Config becomes portable across local, test and production. Rungs 2 and 3 together are how our production gateways run.

Each rung fixes the leak of the one below it. You need to know which rung you're on. Rung 0, hardcoded. In the repo, in history, in every fork. The rung you never stand on. Rung 1, .env plus interpolation. Out of Git, still visible to docker inspect. Where the labs have lived so far. Rung 2, file-based secrets. A file, not an env var, filled per environment. Works the same in Compose and Kubernetes. Rung 3, secret providers. Config stores a reference that a provider resolves from those files: the production pattern.

05

Rung 1: .env files and Compose interpolation, and where they leak

  • .env is gitignored; .env.example is committed. The example documents every variable with a safe placeholder. Every lab ships one.
  • Compose interpolates ${VAR:-default} at parse time: safe defaults for the lab, real values from your .env.
  • The ceiling: the value still lands in the container's environment, visible in docker inspect, docker compose config and to any code that can dump env.
# docker-compose.yaml: this lab's starting point
environment:
  GATEWAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: "${GATEWAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD_LOCAL:-password}"
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-lab06-postgres-pw}"

# where the leak shows:
docker inspect lab06-timescaledb \
  | grep POSTGRES_PASSWORD        # plaintext
VerdictPerfectly fine for a laptop lab. Not where you stop for shared test and production machines: that's rung 2.
06

Rung 2, file-based secrets: a file, not an env var

# docker-compose.yaml
secrets:
  postgres_password:
    file: ./secrets/postgres_password.txt   # gitignored

services:
  timescaledb:
    secrets: [postgres_password]
    environment:
      # official postgres image: _FILE suffix
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/postgres_password
  • Not in docker inspect, not in the process env: the value only exists as a mounted file the process reads at startup.
  • Portable. Compose secrets:, Kubernetes secret volumes and plain bind mounts all end at a small read-only file at a known path. Ignition's secret provider reads it directly.
  • Clean handover to infra. The repo commits paths and names (plus *.example dummies); infra fills the real files per environment. Our production repo ships committed dummy values for local test, so a fresh clone just works.
  • CI can write these files too: a deploy workflow turns GitHub secrets into password files for the gateway container. More on that later in this part.

Ignition 8.3 secret providers: embedded and referenced secrets

07

Embedded vs referenced secrets

Embedded secret

  • The value is encrypted by this gateway and stored inside its own config.
  • Fine for one hand-managed gateway: set it once in the UI, done.
  • The catch: the ciphertext only decrypts on the gateway that produced it. On a fresh container it is a broken reference.
  • For a pipeline that promotes the same config from local to production: a dead end, unless you manage the keys yourself (the exception, later in this part).

Referenced secret

  • Config stores a reference: "get MSSQL_PASSWORD from provider PlantSecrets", never the value.
  • A file-type secret provider resolves it at runtime from a file: rungs 2 and 3 snap together at /run/secrets/<name>.
  • Our production setup: one file-type provider, about 16 named secrets, every DB connection and auth profile pointing at it by name.
  • Committed config holds no secret material: diff it, review it, deploy it anywhere.
Rule of thumbEmbedded = pet gateway. Referenced = pipeline. If a gateway's config is in Git (after labs 04 and 05, yours is), its secrets should be referenced.
08

One referenced config resolves a different value on each gateway

database-connection config.json, committed
"password": {
  "type": "Referenced",
  "data": {
    "providerName": "PlantSecrets",
    "secretName": "MSSQL_PASSWORD"
  }
}
a name, not a value
local/run/secrets/MSSQL_PASSWORD holds a committed dummy value, so a fresh clone just works
testthe same path holds the file infra filled on the test host
productionthe same path holds the production value, which only production ever holds
You already use this model in CIOne workflow file, and the lab06-gateway-test and lab06-gateway-production GitHub environments each supply their own IGNITION_API_KEY. Referenced secrets bring the same idea inside the gateway.
09

Create a file-type secret provider in the 8.3 gateway UI

Type File

Each secret is a name pointing at a file the gateway reads when it needs it: POSTGRES_PASSWORD to /run/secrets/postgres_password. The provider holds paths, never values.

Type Internal

You type the value into the gateway, which stores it encrypted under its own keys. The connection holds a reference, but the ciphertext only decrypts on that gateway, like an embedded secret. Stretch S1 breaks it on test.

Then re-point the connectionA secret provider is ordinary 8.3 config (ignition/secret-provider). The connection's password changes from Embedded (the value, encrypted, in the connection) to Referenced (provider plus secret name).
secret-provider/LabSecrets/config.json
# what lands on disk
"profile":  { "type": "file" },
"settings": { "files": {
  "POSTGRES_PASSWORD": {
    "filePath": "/run/secrets/postgres_password",
    "fileType": "CLEARTEXT" } } }
10

Move the provider to core and point every deployment mode's password at it

  • The UI saves into the active mode's collection. The local gateway runs -Dignition.config.mode=local-development, so a new provider lands in resources/local-development/, which never deploys. Move it to core: that is what test and production inherit.
  • Every override has its own password field. TimescaleDB has local-development, test and production overrides: re-point the password in each, or that mode keeps its old embedded secret. Create Override in the connection adds one for another mode.
What test resolves
externalthencorethentestneverlocal-development
# where it must live, and where the passwords are
resources/core/ignition/secret-provider/LabSecrets/
resources/core/.../TimescaleDB/config.json        # Referenced
resources/test/.../TimescaleDB/config.json        # Referenced too:
resources/production/.../TimescaleDB/config.json  # each override
resources/local-development/.../TimescaleDB/...   # has its own field
Check with git, not with the UIAfter every UI change, git status tells you which collection it went into. Green locally proves nothing about test.
11

Secrets in GitHub Actions: scoped per environment, kept out of logs

  • Environment-scoped, not repo-wide. lab06-gateway-production holds the production values; a PR build against test can't even see them. Add required reviewers on the production environment for a human gate.
  • Masking is a seatbelt, not a licence. Actions replaces known secret values with *** in logs, but don't echo them, don't set -x around them, don't write them into artifacts.
  • Forks don't get secrets. pull_request runs from forks see empty secrets by design: one more reason deploys trigger on push or a tag, never on a PR.
# lab06-deploy.yml
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, lab06]
    environment: lab06-gateway-test   # scoping
Neverrun: echo ${{ secrets.X }}, and never interpolate a secret straight into a shell command line. Pass it through env: and write it with printf, so it stays out of the run log.
12

The deploy workflow turns GitHub secrets into secret files in the gateway

  1. GitHub secretone source of truth, per environment
  2. Materializefile in the workspace, umask 177 before the value lands
  3. Shippre-wired step copies it to /run/secrets/ in the container
  4. Providerreads the file by name
  5. Referencein the committed config
The files live in that containerA recreated container starts without them until the next deploy writes them again. Our production boot script does the same thing: umask and chmod 0600 before the value is written.
- name: Materialize secret files
  env:
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.POSTGRES_PASSWORD }}
  run: |
    umask 177                    # files land 0600
    mkdir -p secrets
    printf '%s' "$POSTGRES_PASSWORD" \
      > secrets/postgres_password.txt
- name: Ship secret files into gateway container
  run: |                         # (abridged)
    docker exec -u root "$IGNITION_CONTAINER" \
      install -d -o 2003 -g 0 -m 750 /run/secrets
    docker cp secrets/postgres_password.txt \
      "$IGNITION_CONTAINER:/run/secrets/postgres_password"
13

The never-commit list for an Ignition repo

  • .env, any real one. (.env.example with placeholders: yes, please.)
  • secrets/ contents: only the *.example files are tracked.
  • PATs and API keys: ghp_..., runner registration tokens, gateway API keys.
  • Gateway backups (.gwbk) from real systems: users, DB connections and keystores in one bundle.
  • Keystores and TLS private keys: ssl.pfx, metro-keystore, *.p12.
# .gitignore: the relevant lines
.env
secrets/*
!secrets/*.example
*.gwbk

# the secret scan (plus the CI linters)
./scripts/validate.sh # no secrets where they shouldn't be = green
Enforcement, not vigilancescripts/validate.sh runs a secret scan (tracked files under secrets/, known values in the payload) and lab06-ci.yml repeats it on every PR: a leaked key fails the build before a reviewer sees it. A gitleaks job over every commit of a PR is stretch S3.
14

The one exception: committed ciphertexts, if you manage the gateway keys

  1. Key CLI tool8.3 ships ignition-secrets-tool.sh
  2. Root key and KEKsJSON files under data/config/ignition/keys/
  3. Same keys everywhereinfra distributes them, the way redundant pairs already share them
  4. Ciphertext travelscommitted embedded secrets decrypt on every gateway
The keys become the secretAn alternative to file-based secrets, not a shortcut: infra distributes the keys, and they never go in Git.
DocsSecrets Management Key CLI Tool. Stretch S1 puts this trade-off next to Part 1's referenced secrets.

Part 2: version and deploy the database schema with your screens

15

Schema drift: a screen ships without the table it needs

What Git deploys to production
Perspective view "DowntimeLog"
  named query: SELECT reason, minutes
    FROM downtime_log ...
new screen, shipped
What the production database has
ignition_production=# \dt
  batch_log      present
  recipe_params  present
  downtime_log   missing
created by hand on test only, three weeks ago
  • "Worked on test." Because someone manually created the table on test. Production was never told. The screen errors on release night.
  • No history. Who changed the column type? When? Why? Hand-run SQL has no git log.
  • The fix is the same as always: schema changes become files in the repo, reviewed in the same PR as the screens that need them, applied by the pipeline.
16

db-init/: bootstrap, not deployment

# docker-compose.yaml: the timescaledb service
volumes:
  - ./db-init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro

# db-init/01-create-env-databases.sh (runs psql)
CREATE DATABASE ignition_test;
CREATE DATABASE ignition_production;
CREATE ROLE reporting LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
The one rulePostgres runs /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d once, on first init of an empty data volume. Volume already exists? Nothing runs. Ever again.
  • Great for: creating the databases, the app user, extensions: the "day zero" shape of a fresh environment.
  • Useless for: changing a database that already has data. Editing db-init/ after first boot changes nothing on any running environment.
  • The trap: "I added the table to db-init and it worked!", because you also wiped your volume. Production doesn't get its volume wiped.
  • So: day-zero shape goes in db-init/. Every change after that is a migration.
17

Migrations: numbered SQL files, applied in order, tracked in the database

db-migration/migrate/
0001_create_production_kpi.up.sql + .down.sql
CREATE TABLE production_kpi (...);
INSERT INTO production_kpi ... ;  -- seed rows
0002_add_downtime_log.up.sql + .down.sql
CREATE TABLE downtime_log (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  reason TEXT, minutes INT, area TEXT);
0003_downtime_add_shift.up.sql + .down.sql
ALTER TABLE downtime_log
  ADD COLUMN shift TEXT;
migrate up
applies what's missing, in order
schema_migrations, inside each database
0001create production kpi: applied on test and production
0002add downtime log: applied on test and production
0003downtime add shift: pending on production, applies on the next deploy
The rules, from the production repo's docs/MIGRATIONS.mdAlways pairs (up applies, down undoes). Never edit a migration after it deployed anywhere: fix mistakes with a new number. Each database tracks its own position in schema_migrations, so every environment catches up at its own pace.

We use golang-migrate, like our file-based production repo. Build the ledger step by step. 0001, the first pair. The production_kpi table this lab ships with, as an up/down pair. 0002, a change. A new table, as a new pair. 0001 is never edited: history only appends. 0003, another change. Each pair is numbered; order is the contract. migrate up compares the files with schema_migrations in the target DB and applies only what's missing. Versioned, append-only, paired, tracked per environment. It's Git for your schema.

18

The deploy pipeline, now with a database step before the screens ship

  1. Validatealready done on the PR by lab06-ci.yml; the deploy does not repeat it
  2. Checkoutthe merged commit on main, or the lab06-v* tag
  3. Migrate DBnew: migrate up against the target environment's database; fails, run stops
  4. Ship filesprune per .deployignore, docker cp into the gateway
  5. ScanPOST /scan: projects and config, no restart
  6. VerifyStatusPing answers, the gateway is up
Why migrate before shipOld screens tolerate a new table; new screens don't tolerate a missing one. A half-failed run leaves production on old screens plus new, unused schema: a safe place to stop.
On failureA failing migrate step fails the whole run: no screens ship. Fix forward with a new migration. Our file-based production pipeline runs migrations after the scan, with continueOnError: spot what can go wrong with that in the We-do.
19

Rename a column without breaking a live screen: expand, then contract

Deploy 1

Expand

-- 0003_downtime_add_cause.up.sql
ALTER TABLE downtime_log
  ADD COLUMN cause TEXT;
UPDATE downtime_log
  SET cause = reason;   -- backfill
-- .down.sql:
-- ALTER TABLE downtime_log
--   DROP COLUMN cause;

Old screens still read reason and keep working; nothing reads cause yet.

Deploy 2

Switch

-- the screens read the new column
SELECT cause, minutes, area
  FROM downtime_log ...

A normal screen PR. Both columns exist, so the deploy is safe in either order.

Deploy 3

Contract

-- 0004_downtime_drop_reason.up.sql
ALTER TABLE downtime_log
  DROP COLUMN reason;
-- .down.sql: ADD COLUMN reason TEXT;
--   UPDATE downtime_log
--   SET reason = cause;

Only once every environment runs the new screens, production included.

One-step renameRENAME COLUMN in a single migration: the migrate step runs first, and every screen still selecting reason errors until the ship step lands. On a slow or failed run, that is your outage. Stretch S2 practises the safe way.

Part 3: version and deploy third-party modules and JAR files instead of installing them by hand

20

Third-party modules: commit the .modl and load it from a folder

  1. Commit the binarythe .modl goes in third-party-modules/, tracked like any file (Git LFS in the real repos; these are small enough to commit directly)
  2. The folder is wiredevery gateway's compose command: passes the external modules folder flag; the gateway loads from it at boot
  3. Ship it like everything elsefile-based: the pipeline copies the folder to the gateway host. Image-based: one COPY layer, like yesterday's Dockerfile
# docker-compose.yaml, every gateway's command: (already there, nothing to change)
-Dignition.gateway.externalModulesFolder=/third-party-modules
# /third-party-modules is where the repo folder is mounted in the container
Same pattern in both production reposThe binary lives in Git, a JVM flag points the gateway at the folder, and license acceptance is data, not a click. Next slide.
21

Accept the license in config: the gateway writes the fingerprint and hash for you

  1. List the module id in all three compose env vars.
  2. Add a minimal entry to modules.json: only filename and onStartup.
  3. Boot once. The gateway accepts headlessly and writes certFingerprint and licenseAgreementHash back into modules.json. You never type or guess them.
  4. Commit what it wrote. Now a fresh gateway with no env vars accepts from config alone.
# 1: compose env vars: the module id in all three
GATEWAY_MODULES_ENABLED:  ..., com.mussonindustrial.embr.charts
ACCEPT_MODULE_LICENSES:   ..., com.mussonindustrial.embr.charts
ACCEPT_MODULE_CERTS:      ..., com.mussonindustrial.embr.charts

# 2: modules.json: you write only these two lines
"com.mussonindustrial.embr.charts": {
  "filename": "/third-party-modules/Embr-Charts-Ignition83-4.0.1.modl",
  "onStartup": "enabled"
}

# 3: boot once: the gateway ADDS these itself
  "certFingerprint": "e5a3cf3f06627c175b68b0122ac8f2c3f9c992e2",
  "licenseAgreementHash": 3266212556
# 4: commit them: fresh gateways accept headlessly, every boot
22

What an unaccepted module and a wiped data volume do to a gateway's first boot

Enabled but not accepted

A module in GATEWAY_MODULES_ENABLED without its acceptance (the env lists or the derived modules.json fields) parks the gateway at commissioning: StatusPing says "details":"COMMISSIONING" until a human clicks accept. On a server nobody watches, that gateway is down.

Wiped volume, surviving config tree

Commissioning finds the committed security-properties but no internal identity on disk, plays safe: it creates a temp user source and identity provider and rewrites security-properties to use them. That drops the APIToken permissions: every scan now gets 403.

The real-world lessonA fresh data volume runs commissioning on first boot. Wiping it while the config tree survives is how you lock yourself out. scripts/setup.sh choreographs a first boot to avoid it; a bare docker compose up on a wiped volume does not. Part 3's negative test makes you live through it once.
23

Recover a gateway stuck at commissioning, in this order

  1. Acceptance backlet the gateway reach RUNNING first: until then the temp identity does not exist, so there is nothing to undo
  2. Undo commissioningrestore security-properties from git, delete the temp folders
  3. Restart and scanHTTP 200 again
# 1: acceptance back, boot to RUNNING
git checkout -- docker-compose.yaml services/modules.json
docker compose up -d gateway-local-development
# 2: undo what commissioning did, then restart
git checkout -- services/config/resources/core/ignition/security-properties/
rm -rf services/config/resources/core/ignition/{user-source,identity-provider}/temp
docker restart lab06-gateway-local-development
./scripts/scan.sh          # HTTP 200 again
24

JAR files: JDBC drivers are config resources, other libraries go on the classpath

Kind 1

JDBC drivers: part of the 8.3 config tree

  • In 8.3 a database driver is a config resource: the JAR sits inside the resource folder, next to its config.json.
  • Committed and deployed in production: config/resources/core/ignition/database-driver/PostgreSQL/postgresql-42.7.2.jar, with resource.json listing the JAR in its "files".
  • It ships with the ordinary config copy. Deploy the config tree and the driver arrives with it.
Kind 2

Library JARs: on the gateway classpath

  • Java libraries your gateway scripts call. Our image-based production repo ships amqp-client (RabbitMQ) and an SMB client, with their pinned dependency JARs.
  • They live in modules/jar/ with a README recording where each JAR came from (the Maven Central command), and get copied to lib/core/gateway/.
  • The classpath is read at boot: shipping a JAR means a restart. Pin the versions, commit the binaries: the gateway has no package manager, your repo is the lockfile.
25

This lab's library JAR: commons-csv, from the repo to a gateway script

  1. In the repojar-files/jar/commons-csv-1.14.1.jar
  2. On the classpathcopied to lib/core/gateway/
  3. Restartlibrary JARs load at boot, like modules
  4. Import itfrom any gateway-scoped script, Perspective bindings included
# a gateway-scoped script, once the JAR is on the classpath
from org.apache.commons.csv import CSVFormat
Why commons-csvThe Ignition image does not bundle it. commons-lang3, commons-text and guava it does, so those import fine without you shipping anything. Stretch S4 ships it through the pipeline and puts it on a screen.
One rule covers all of Part 3Modules and JARs are deployable state, exactly like a view or a config file. If the gateway needs it to run, it lives in the repo, travels through the pipeline, and a fresh gateway comes up complete with no hands on it.
26

Perspective property bindings and script transforms, and what the CI linter accepts

  • Property binding: a component property follows another property by path, for example view.custom.line. Ticking bidirectional lets an input write back into it.
  • Script transform: Jython that runs on the gateway after the binding, gets the bound value and returns what the property shows. It is a function body, so imports go inside it; the gateway's classpath decides what imports.
  • No sibling paths. ign-lint's BadComponentReferenceRule rejects ../TextField.props.text: share state through a view custom property (text field bidirectional to view.custom.line, label bound to it).
  • Warnings fail the job too. Keep custom property names plain lowerCamel words (line; NamePatternRule flags csvLine). The lab's .config/.ignition-pylintrc already allows the import inside a transform.
# view.json, abridged: the label's binding
"custom": { "line": "" },
...
"meta": { "name": "Label" },
"propConfig": { "props.text": { "binding": {
  "type": "property",
  "config": { "path": "view.custom.line" },
  "transforms": [{ "type": "script", "code":
    from org.apache.commons.csv import CSVFormat
    from java.io import StringReader
    records = CSVFormat.DEFAULT.parse(
        StringReader(value or "")).getRecords()
    return " | ".join(records[0]) if records else ""
  }] } } }
